paper_title: DAGFormer: Global Topology Prediction for Transformer Cross-Layer Connections

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: We propose DAGFormer, a Transformer language model whose cross-layer connections are planned by a jointly trained topology predictor. Beyond the residual connections in a standard Transformer, DAGFormer adds direct connections from earlier layers to later ones, and the predictor controls the strength of every connection based on input tokens. Unlike existing cross-layer routing architectures, which set each layer's connections separately, DAGFormer plans the routing of the whole model at once. On matched OLMo-2 pairs from 75M to 1B parameters, DAGFormer lowers WikiText-2 perplexity by 17% to 25% over the vanilla Transformer, and a 1B DAGFormer trained on 5B tokens outperforms the vanilla model trained on 10B. Against four routing baselines with the same data and budget, it reaches the lowest perplexity at 75M, 300M and 1B. The gain carries over to 13 commonsense, science, reading and math evaluation tasks (2.0 to 2.5 points higher mean accuracy at 300M and 1B) and to instruction finetuning (63% to 70% AlpacaEval win rate against the vanilla Transformer, leading every routing baseline), and under structured pruning DAGFormer degrades the least in five of six settings.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: A Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017) composes its layers through residual connections (He et al., 2016): every attention head and MLP reads the same running sum and writes back into it. Mechanistic analyses describe this residual stream as the communication channel between model components (Elhage et al., 2021). Its bandwidth is shared by every layer, so which earlier computation layer can read is fixed by design: late layer sees an early result only inside sum to which every intermediate layer has added its own. * Equal contribution. line of work relaxes this fixed connectivity. Dense connections (Huang et al., 2017) and depthweighted averaging with learned static weights (Pagliardini et al., 2024) let layer read earlier layers outputs directly. Hyper-connections (Zhu et al., 2025) widen the residual stream into several streams whose mixing weights are learned and, in the dynamic variant, input-dependent, and mHC (Xie et al., 2026) constrains those mixing matrices so the scheme trains stably at scale. Multiway dynamic dense connections (Xiao et al., 2025) compute input-dependent weights over all earlier layers outputs, separately for the query, key, value and residual inputs of block. Each token can then follow its own path through the layers, and these models reach the loss of Transformers trained with substantially more budget (Zhu et al., 2025; Xiao et al., 2025). All of the dynamic variants above, however, make the same design choice: routing is local. Each layer carries its own router, which reads the hidden state entering that layer and decides what that layer reads and, in hyper-connections and mHC, where its output is written. The cross-layer routing topology is therefore assembled greedily, one layer at time, and no module takes global view of it. Consequently, cross-layer coordination cannot be planned explicitly from the input, and the topology cannot be inspected as an individual object. In this paper, we propose DAGFormer, where the global routing topology is predicted with separate module that reads only the input tokens, before the backbone processes each token. DAGFormer implements this idea on an OLMo-2 backbone (Walsh et al., 2025) with added cross-layer connections on attention heads. Instead of reading the running residual stream, each attention head computes its query, key and value from weighted mixtures of the embedding and all earlier layer outputs. Additionally, an auxiliary local refinement, zero-initialized, lets each layer correct the predicted weights of its own heads from its input, so the predictor plans the graph and each layer refines its rows of it. To study this model architecture, we train matched pairs of the standard OLMo-2 Transformer (vanilla Transformer) and DAGFormer from 75M to 1B parameters on Dolma (Soldaini et al., 2024), charging the routing cost in every compute comparison. DAGFormer is better at every size and at equal compute, and 1B DAGFormer beats the 1B vanilla Transformer trained on twice as many tokens. It also beats four routing baselines trained with the same pipeline at every size but 150M, and the gain carries over to evaluation tasks and instruction finetuning. Ablations show that the shared predictor carries most of the gain, and under structured pruning DAGFormer loses the least of all baselines in five of six settings. Our contributions are as follows: OLMo-2 backbone from scratch (Section 2). matched scaling study from 75M to 1B with the routing cost charged and with DenseFormer, hyper-connection, mHC and MUDDFormer baselines on the same pipeline, carried through instruction finetuning and instruction-following evaluation (Section 3). Ablations of the routing source and structured-pruning study showing that the learned topology makes models degrade more gracefully, without re-planning by the predictor (Sections 4, 5 and 6).

sections.title: 3.1 Data
sections.content: All pretraining uses Dolma v1.7 (Soldaini et al., 2024). Three tokenizations were used (a 12B-token slice for the 75M to 600M pairs, local rebuild of it, and 21B-token one for the 300M and 1B pairs), so every final checkpoint is re-evaluated on the same held-out sets: WikiText-2 (Merity et al., 2017), held-out slice of MathInstruct (Yue et al., 2024), GSM8K solutions (Cobbe et al., 2021), and source-balanced Dolma set drawn from files no training corpus consumed (Appendix B). WikiText2 is the primary metric; the balanced set gives the same orderings with gaps 10% to 25% smaller. For instruction finetuning we use two datasets: Alpaca (Taori et al., 2023) in its cleaned release plus Dolly (Conover et al., 2023), about 67K singleturn instructions, and the smol-smoltalk subset of SmolTalk (Allal et al., 2025), about 460K conversations, the mix used to finetune SmolLM2 at 135M and 360M parameters. The held-out instruction data of Table 3 are 1% of Alpaca plus Dolly and the test split of smol-smoltalk.

sections.title: 3.3 Main results
sections.content: DAGFormer has the lowest WikiText-2 loss of all baselines at every size but 150M  (Table 1)  . It is 0.18 to 0.29 nats below the vanilla Transformer at every size (17% to 25% lower perplexity) and 0.1 to 0.2 nats below the strongest routing baseline at 75M, 300M and 1B; at 150M MUDDFormer is 0.04 nats lower (Section 6). The gap to the vanilla Transformer opens early in training (Figure 2c) and holds on the other held-out sets, second corpus and seed, and across learning rates (Appendix C.4, Table 13). On the 13 downstream evaluation tasks, DAGFormer has the highest mean accuracy of all models at both sizes we tested  (Table 2)  : 2.0 to 2.5 points above the vanilla Transformer and 0.7 to 0.8 points above the strongest routing baseline. It also leads on the commonsense, science and reading tasks and has the best mean rank at both sizes; on math, where MathQA and GSM8K are close to chance, mHC is 0.1 points ahead. At 1B with 10B tokens, DAGFormer is ahead of the vanilla Transformer on all 13 tasks. We further evaluate the instruction-finetuned models on held-out instruction data and on commonly used instruction-following benchmarks  (Table 3)  . DAGFormer has the lowest negative loglikelihood on held-out instruction data of all models at every size and under both recipes, 0.15 to 0.19 nats below the vanilla Transformer and 0.04 to 0.06 below the strongest routing baseline. sections.content: For each family we fit = + AN α to the final WikiText-2 loss against backbone parameters and = + KCγ against training compute C, routing cost included, with the irreducible loss shared by the two families (Figure 2). We share because it estimates the entropy of the evaluation text, which does not depend on the architecture. At equal training compute the margin is larger at 300M and 1B than at the smaller sizes: on the vanilla compute fit, the vanilla Transformer needs 1.2 to 1.4 DAGFormers training compute to reach its loss at 75M and 150M, and 1.7 to 2.0 at 300M and 1B. DAGFormers fitted exponents are also larger (0.56 against 0.48 for parameters, 0.30 against 0.27 for compute), so on the fit the compute multiplier keeps growing (1.9 at 1020 FLOPs and 2.3 at 1021), although in each fit the two exponents differ by about one standard error and nothing beyond our largest run is tested. Without any fit, the 1B DAGFormer trained on 5B tokens beats the 1B vanilla Transformer trained on 10B tokens at about the same training compute, on WikiText-2, MathInstruct and GSM8K. Extra parameters explain most of the gain at the smallest size and less than half at the larger one. Vanilla Transformers given DAGFormers routing parameters as extra width close 70 to 89% of the gap at 75M but only 4 to 42% at 150M, extra depth closes less, and DAGFormer stays ahead of every control on every held-out set  (Table 4)  .

sections.title: 4.2 Where the gain comes from
sections.content: The predictor carries most of the gain, and the refinement completes it. The routing-source ablation varies only where α comes from in one 75M backbone (Table 14, Appendix C.6). The predictor alone, which never sees hidden state, recovers about 90% of DAGFormers gain over the vanilla Transformer, and adding the refinement gives the best result on every held-out set. Sharing matters: independent per-layer predictors reading the same tokens recover under 80%, with 7M more parameters. The refinement is cheap, under 0.5% of DAGFormers forward multiply-accumulates, and unlike the per-layer routers of hyper-connections and MUDDFormer, which produce layers weights on their own, it corrects the predictors plan per attention head. DAGFormers cost lies instead in projecting every earlier output through each layers query, key and value weights before mixing (Appendix A), where MUDDFormer mixes the hidden states first and projects once.

sections.title: 5 Structured pruning
sections.content: If the benefit is structural, heads that read many earlier layers should lose less when units are removed, without the routers re-planning. We finetune every model of Table 1 up to 300M from its own checkpoint on MathInstruct (Yue et al., 2024) and, during finetuning, permanently remove attention heads and MLP channels (two of CoFis unit types; Xia et al., 2022) by first-order Taylor importance on unit gates (Michel et al., 2019; Molchanov et al., 2019) on gradual cubic schedule (Zhu and Gupta, 2018), followed by recovery steps. Routers are never pruned, and we report backbone sparsity. DAGFormer loses the least of all models in five of the six settings  (Table 5)  . With half the heads and channels removed, it degrades less than the vanilla Transformer and every routing baseline at every size, and remains about as good as or better than the unpruned vanilla Transformer. With 70% removed, it degrades the least at 150M and 300M; at 75M the vanilla Transformer, DenseFormer and both hyper-connection variants lose less, although DAGFormers pruned loss is still the lowest. MUDDFormer, the closest dynamic design, loses the most at every size and sparsity. No model relies on re-planning its routing: freezing DAGFormers predictor, or the baselines routers, during pruning barely changes the result  (Table 23)  . The advantage lies in the sources each head can draw on (Appendix G); with units removed at random both families lose much more and the gap shrinks at 75M (Appendix C.8).

sections.title: 6 Discussion
sections.content: Token dependence. Most of DAGFormers gain lies in the learned graph, set of cross-layer connections and their weights, rather than in re-planning it for every token: the predictors output can be replaced by its per-position mean at almost no cost (Appendix D), and the predictor alone recovers about 90% of the gain (Section 4.2). Input dependence, which dynamic cross-layer architectures cite to motivate their routers, matters mostly while the graph is learned: static weights trained directly (DenseFormer, static hyper-connections, an inputfree table) recover little of it (Appendix C.2). At inference the trained models still rely on the refinements per-token corrections, and sparsifying the graph post hoc is costly (Appendix E); distilling it into fixed topology that dense kernel can execute is future work. sections.title: 7 Related work
sections.content: Cross-layer connectivity. After highway and residual skips (Srivastava et al., 2015; He et al., 2016), DenseNet (Huang et al., 2017) connected every layer to every earlier one, and transparent attention (Bapna et al., 2018), ELMo (Peters et al., 2018), DenseFormer (Pagliardini et al., 2024) and LAuReL (Menghani et al., 2025) learn static weights over layer outputs. Hyper-connections (Zhu et al., 2025) widen the residual stream into several streams whose connections can depend on the incoming hidden state, and mHC (Xie et al., 2026) constrains their residual-mixing matrices to be doubly stochastic. MUDDFormer (Xiao et al., 2025) generates per-position query, key, value and residual weights from each layers hidden state; DAGFormer shares this decomposition (per head for q, k, v) but plans the weights of all layers with one predictor over the tokens, which each layer refines per head from its input. Conditional computation. Conditional computation runs part of network per input (Bengio et al., 2013; Han et al., 2022): mixture-of-experts layers send each token to few experts (Jacobs et al., 1991; Shazeer et al., 2017; Lepikhin et al., 2021; Fedus et al., 2022; Zhou et al., 2022), adaptivedepth models halt or exit early (Graves, 2016; Dehghani et al., 2019; Elbayad et al., 2020; Schuster et al., 2022), and mixture-of-depths lets tokens skip whole blocks (Raposo et al., 2024). BlockDrop (Wu et al., 2018), the closest analogue to planned topology, picks all blocks an image skips with one policy network instead of per-layer gates (Wang et al., 2018; Veit and Belongie, 2020). These methods choose how much computation an input receives; DAGFormer keeps it fixed and chooses which earlier results each layer reads.

sections.title: 8 Conclusion
sections.content: We introduced DAGFormer, Transformer whose cross-layer connections are planned by one predictor over the input tokens, trained jointly with the backbone. From 75M to 1B it lowers loss at every size and at equal compute, beats four routing baselines at every size but 150M, carries its gain to evaluation tasks and instruction finetuning, and degrades the least under structured pruning in five of six settings. Most of the gain lies in the learned graph, which the separate predictor makes an object that can be inspected and intervened on.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: Scale and seeds. Our largest model has 1B parameters trained on 5 to 10B tokens, below its compute-optimal budget. Every pretraining run but the 300M pair is single seed. Repeating the 300M pair with second pretraining seed changes models held-out NLL by up to 0.08 nats per token (the vanilla Transformer on GSM8K solutions; at most 0.03 on WikiText-2; Appendix C.4), so smaller differences are noise; the pruning cells are single runs too. Cost. Routing costs 1.18 to 2.13 the vanilla Transformers FLOPs per token in the order used for training, and the trained models rely on the refinements per-token corrections, so they cannot run with fixed topology without retraining. Comparisons. MUDDFormer trained with our recipe beats DAGFormer at 150M and loses at the other sizes, each single seed, so loss alone does not settle that comparison; the 1B baselines are trained at 5B tokens only, the parametermatched vanilla Transformer controls exist at 75M and 150M, and only the 75M pair was swept over learning rates. Evaluation. Models of this size sit near chance on harder benchmarks, and single LLM judge scored the chat and AlpacaEval comparisons. Interpretability and scale. We intervene on the learned graph only as whole and read it only in aggregate; whether its input-dependent part can be named, and whether the gains persist beyond 1B parameters, are left to follow-up work.

sections.title: A Compute accounting
sections.content: Forward MACs per token for the vanilla Transformer backbone are (cid:80)L l=1(4D2 + 3DI) + plus attention over the context (2T per layer at sequence length ), with the model width, the MLP width and the vocabulary. In the project-then-mix order used in training, DAGFormer adds, at every routed layer 2, the projection of l1 extra sources through the fused q, k, weights ((l1) 3D2), the per-head mixing sums (l(3D + D)), the predictor (embedding lookup, 2 encoder layers of width 256, trunk and per-layer heads) and the local refinement networks (D 128 + 128 (3H+1) per layer). Training FLOPs are 6 the forward MACs times tokens: the 6N per token estimate of Kaplan et al. (2020) (a backward pass costs about twice the forward), applied to all the forward MACs above, so the unembedding, attention-context and routing terms that 6N leaves out are included. The ratios are 1.18 (75M), 1.33 (150M), 1.65 (300M) and 2.13 (1B); the predictor itself is under 2% of the total, the source projections dominate. Table 6 gives the measured training cost of every model of Table 1: forward and backward passes over 2 sequences of 1024 tokens with bf16 weights, as in pretraining, on one A100-40GB, every model compiled with torch.compile (median of 20 iterations after warm-up, no optimizer step). Every cell, here and in Table 1, is the fastest of two runs; the runs agree within 1% in every cell but one, the 75M vanilla Transformer, timed first in its job (6%). The baselines are measured at random initialization, since the weights do not change the speed. DAGFormer trains at 1.44 to 1.77 the vanilla Transformers time in the faster of its two orders; under 300M mHC is the slowest to train. Replacing the predictor by constant table changes DAGFormers time by 1 to 3%. At inference DAGFormer keeps every layers output for the later layers to mix, so its peak memory for 8 sequences of 1024 tokens is 1.9 vs 1.8 GB (75M) to 9.1 vs 4.2 GB (1B), close to MUDDFormer, which also keeps them (8.7 GB at 1B). Without compilation every routed model is slower, the baselines most (hyper-connections 2.3 to 2.8, mHC 2.3 to 3.2 at inference; experiments/scaling/inference_cost.json). A.1 Two exact computation orders (cid:80) j<l α(l) j<l α(l) q,h,jW The q, k, projections have no bias, so for each head the projection of mixture equals the mixture of projections, q,h,jXj = (cid:80) Xj (likewise for and v), and DAGFormer can compute layers inputs in either order. Project-then-mix, used in training, runs one fused q, k, GEMM over the stacked sources: (l1) 3D2 extra MACs at layer l, at full GEMM efficiency. Mix-then-project first forms one mixture of the sources per head for each of q, k, (3HlD MACs) and then applies each heads slice of the projection, so the whole model needs only 1.02 to 1.04 the vanilla Transformers FLOPs; in exchange it writes and reads 3H vectors of width per token and layer and runs narrow GEMMs instead of one wide one, so it is bound by memory traffic. Per token and layer, the first order spends about D/H extra MACs, the head width, for every value the second order moves: 64 up to 300M and 128 at 1B. Consistent with this, projecting first is faster at inference up to 300M (1.49 vs 1.68 the vanilla Transformer at 75M, 1.61 vs 1.77 at 150M, 1.89 vs 1.93 at 300M) and mixing first at 1B (1.81 vs 2.38); in training the two are within 3% up to 300M and mixing first is faster at 1B (1.65 vs 2.17). Both orders give the same logits up to 104 in fp32 at every size (scripts/check_mix_order.py). Table 1 and Table 6 report the faster order per size and measure. The modular variant projects 2l1 sources per layer and costs 1.33 to 2.30. Held-out sets The 21B-token tokenizations held-out tail is the last windows of its last shard, and the eight tokenization workers each took contiguous block of Dolmas source-sorted file list, so that tail is templated instruction and Wikipedia text only; 21Bcorpus runs score about 2.2 nats on it while scoring about 3.5 on WikiText-2. The tail is used only to compare runs within that corpus (the 300M threeway and the 1B pairs, where all models see the same training mix). The 1.7B-token slice used by the locality ablation has similar single-source tail. All cross-corpus numbers in the paper are on WikiText-2, MathInstruct and GSM8K.

sections.title: C Additional tables
sections.content: This appendix gives the complete results that the body summarizes: every stage of the downstream and chat evaluations, the post-hoc baselines and learning rates, the training hyperparameters, every held-out set for the matched pairs, the routingsource ablation and the static substitution, the earlier pruning study, and the chat evaluation by category. C.1 Downstream and chat per stage Table 8 gives the per-task accuracies of Table 2, Table 7 every stage of it and Table 10 every chat comparison, including the second instructionfinetuning seed of the 300M pair. Repeating the 300M instruction finetuning with second seed moves the 12-task mean by at most 0.001 and the routed-minus-vanilla gaps by at most 0.003. Alpaca finetuning leaves the multiple-choice mean within 0.002, SmolTalk lowers it by 0.7 to 1.4 points for every model, and GSM8K bits per byte improve by 0.13 to 0.25 after SmolTalk. sections.title: D The predictor learns a static graph
sections.content: What the predictor contributes is one graph per position, not per-token re-routing. Because it is separate module, we can replace its per-token output by its mean over held-out windows  (Table 20)  . At 300M and 1B the per-position mean costs at most 0.005 nats on WikiText-2 (3.544 vs 3.547; 3.219 vs 3.221 for the 1B at 10B tokens) and single global mean 0.04 to 0.06, while the same replacement of the refinements output costs 0.4 to 0.7 nats, more than the whole gap over the vanilla Transformer. Swapping the predictors output between windows (activation patching; Vig et al., 2020; Meng et al., 2022; Zhang and Nanda, 2024) changes the loss by at most 0.007 nats from 75M to 300M (the refinement: 0.56 to 1.29). The token input is needed to learn the graph, not to apply it. In the predictor-only arm the per-token output carries 0.03 to 0.08 nats, yet replacing it by its position mean costs only 0.01 to 0.02, so the model routes per-token variation through the refinement when it has one. table of the same weights trained from scratch with no input recovers only 17 to 23% of the predictor-only arms gain over the vanilla Transformer (0.04 of 0.18 nats on the own cache, 0.06 of 0.39 on WikiText-2; Table 14), and DenseFormers learned static weights recover as little from 75M to 1B (at most 24%; Table 1). The predictor is thus parameterization that finds good static graph, which Appendix analyses. The averages and swaps above are interventions on computation before its output exists, which ties the design to broader aim. Post-hoc interpretability explains computation only after it has produced its output, whereas generative interpretability asks that models inference pass expose checkpoints that humans can understand and that can be causally intervened on before the output is committed (Yang, 2026). predicted topology meets the second requirement by construction, since the backbone depends on it and replacing it is welldefined intervention; whether it can also be made understandable to humans is question this design opens.

sections.title: G Why reading many layers may soften
sections.content: pruning Figure 3 plots the results of Table 24. head that reads several earlier layers has several routes to the information it needs, so removing one unit removes one route rather than the only one. The frozen-router result is consistent with this reading: the gain needs no re-routing, only the connections that training put in place. The random-pruning control shows its limit, since the advantage shrinks when the removed units are not the least important ones. We have not tested the redundancy hypothesis directly, for instance by counting alternative paths around removed heads.

sections.title: H The modular variant
sections.content: Figure 4 places the modular variant in the scaling plots of Figure 2. In FourWay routing the sources are layer outputs, so the attention-to-MLP edge inside layer, the block-to-everything-downstream edges and the final read-out are fixed. modular variant makes the sources the module outputs (embedding, then each layers attention and MLP outputs) and adds routed MLP input and routed final read-out, so every intermodular edge is predicted; its routing is 2l1 sources per layer and costs 1.33 (75M) to 2.30 (300M) the vanilla Transformers FLOPs. At 300M on the 21B corpus, FourWay beats modular on every held-out set (WikiText-2 3.544 vs 3.628, Dolma tail 2.221 vs 2.268, MathInstruct 2.565 vs 2.616, GSM8K 2.937 vs 3.093), and the modular compute multiplier is 1.15 at 75M and 0.81 to 0.93 at 150M to 300M (its extra FLOPs are not repaid). Modular routing is better in one setting: whole-block pruning scored by the mass of modules routing column, where it beats FourWays Taylor-pruned blocks at 150M (2.015 vs 2.044 nats at third of the blocks removed, 2.130 vs 2.229 at half).
